To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) emotion dysregulation and interpersonal dysfunction are core features of borderline personality disorder; 2) both emotion and interpersonal dysfunction are related to frontolimbic brain dysfunction; 3) the brain systems underlying emotion regulation and interpersonal functioning are highly interrelated and are both affected in borderline personality disorder; and 4) a developmental perspective on the interpersonal context of borderline pathology is necessary to account for the full range of behavioral, cognitive and emotional dysfunctions that are observed in borderline personality disorder.
emotion dysregulation is associated with frontolimbic abnormalities in BPD and that the social baseline model can be used to explain this association.
emotion dysregulation and social dysfunction are both associated with frontolimbic dysregulation and are both important to the understanding of borderline personality disorder (see Figure).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the brain in emotion regulation and the implications of this work for our understanding of borderline pathology.
the development of a comprehensive model of BPD that integrates multiple levels of analysis, including the neurobiological, behavioral, and interpersonal.
the neurobiology and psychopathology of borderline pathology and the role of the social context in both.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BPD is characterized by an impairment in emotion regulation that is mediated by a dysfunctional frontolimbical circuitry.
borderline personality disorder is a disorder characterized by a pervasive impairment of the capacity to self-regulate emotion.
BPD is characterized by a pervasive and chronic dysregulation of the social baseline, and this dysregulation is a core feature of the disorder.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social baseline theory provides a new framework for conceptualizing the neurobiology of borderline pathology.
the social baseline perspective is a useful framework for understanding BPD.

the social baseline perspective provides a framework for understanding how the brain is organized to function in a social context, and that this perspective is particularly useful in understanding the development and maintenance of borderline pathology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
emotion regulation and interpersonal functioning are inextricable.
emotion dysregulation and social baseline theory are important for understanding the development of BPD and its associated symptoms.
the social baseline perspective provides a framework for understanding BPD that accounts for the broad range of dysfunction associated with the disorder.
